details:
**Edict of Fontainebleau (revocation of the Edict of Nantes)**
A 1685 decree by which Louis XIV revoked Henry IV's 1598 Edict of Nantes, which had granted religious toleration to French Protestants (Huguenots). It closed Protestant churches and schools and caused perhaps 200,000 or more Huguenots to flee France.

**Palace of Versailles and the Hall of Mirrors**
The enormous palace outside Paris that Louis XIV expanded from a hunting lodge and to which he moved his court from the Louvre. Built by architects including Louis Le Vau and Jules Hardouin-Mansart, it features the Hall of Mirrors, the Basin of Neptune, and the Grand Trianon; forcing nobles to live there reduced their independent power.

**The Fronde**
A series of revolts from 1648 to 1653, during Louis XIV's childhood, against royal authority and the chief minister Cardinal Mazarin. It had a "parliamentary" phase led by the Parlement of Paris and a "princely" phase led by nobles such as the Prince of Conde, and was named after the slingshots Parisian crowds used to smash windows.

**Cardinal Mazarin**
The Italian-born chief minister of France during Louis XIV's minority, working alongside the regent Anne of Austria, Louis's mother. He was the main target of the Fronde and arranged Louis's marriage to Maria Theresa of Spain; Louis began his personal rule after Mazarin's death in 1661.

**Jean-Baptiste Colbert**
Louis XIV's finance minister, who rose after the fall of Nicolas Fouquet. He pursued mercantilist policies, building up French industry and trade, and is associated with efforts like luring Venetian glassmakers to France so it no longer depended on Venetian glass imports.

**War of the Spanish Succession**
A war from 1701 to 1714 caused by Louis XIV's attempt to place his grandson Philip of Anjou on the Spanish throne as Philip V. France fought a coalition including England, the Dutch Republic, and Austria and suffered defeats such as Blenheim and Turin; Philip kept the throne but France's power was checked.

**"I am the state" ("L'etat, c'est moi") and the Sun King**
A phrase traditionally attributed to Louis XIV, summing up his absolutism and belief in the divine right of kings, which was promoted by the bishop Jacques-Benigne Bossuet. He called himself the "Sun King," and his reign of 72 years (1643 to 1715) is the longest of any French monarch.

**War of Devolution**
A 1667 to 1668 war in which Louis XIV claimed parts of the Spanish Netherlands through his wife Maria Theresa. The formation of a Triple Alliance of England, the Dutch Republic, and Sweden pushed him to end it with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1668).

**Franco-Dutch War and the Treaty of Nijmegen**
Louis XIV's 1672 to 1678 war against the Dutch Republic, prepared in part by the Secret Treaty of Dover with Charles II of England. It ended with the Treaties of Nijmegen, by which France gained Franche-Comte but returned Maastricht to the Dutch.

**League of Augsburg and the Treaty of Ryswick**
A coalition formed in 1686 by William III of Orange and Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I to counter Louis XIV, later expanded into the Grand Alliance. It fought France in the Nine Years' War (War of the League of Augsburg), which ended with the 1697 Treaty of Ryswick.

**Dragonnades**
A policy of billeting soldiers (dragoons) in the homes of Huguenot families to intimidate them into converting to Catholicism. It accompanied the revocation of the Edict of Nantes and was later followed by the revolt of the Protestant Camisards in the Cevennes.

**Affair of the Poisons**
A scandal at Louis XIV's court from 1677 to 1682 involving accusations of poisoning and witchcraft against aristocrats. It implicated his mistress Madame de Montespan, who was alleged to have used the fortune teller La Voisin to perform black masses and love rituals, and followed the earlier trial of the poisoner Marquise de Brinvilliers.

**Viscount of Turenne and the Battle of the Dunes**
Turenne was one of Louis XIV's greatest marshals. He defeated the Prince of Conde during the Fronde, won the 1658 Battle of the Dunes against Spain, and was killed at the Battle of Salzbach in 1675 during the Franco-Dutch War.

**Code Noir**
A 1685 decree issued by Louis XIV that regulated slavery in the French colonies. It required that enslaved people be baptized as Catholics and also expelled Jews from the colonies.

**Marquis de Vauban and star forts**
Sebastien Le Prestre de Vauban was Louis XIV's chief military engineer. He designed and built a ring of star-shaped fortresses with bastions and ravelins around France's borders and was a master of siege warfare.
